Name: reasoning_working_memory_bottleneck
Title: The Working-Memory Bottleneck: Measuring Live Intermediate-Result Slots to Adaptively Compress Chain-of-Thought
Short Hypothesis: At any point in a chain-of-thought (CoT), a reasoning model maintains a small, bounded set of 'live' intermediate results in its residual stream that are still causally needed for the answer, analogous to a working-memory register file. The size of this live set is measurable online via linear probes, and it is far smaller than the number of tokens the model generates. When the live set is small and stable, subsequent reasoning is mostly bookkeeping and can be compressed; the live-set size gives an interpretable, per-instance signal for how much reasoning remains. Tracking it enables training-free adaptive compression that outperforms uniform-length heuristics.
Related Work: Prior efficient-reasoning work reduces token count via RL length penalties, difficulty routing, sufficiency probes (BLADE), or step pruning (ASAP, CAID). Interpretability work shows intermediate results are encoded in the residual stream (logit/tuned lens, activation patching) and studies 'variable binding' in small settings, but none quantify a live working-memory set that shrinks as reasoning completes, nor use its size as an efficiency signal. My prior proposals target load-bearing tokens, answer commitment, recomputation, overthinking circuits, budget direction, branch precommitment, belief velocity, and per-token depth. This proposal is distinct: it introduces an interpretable, dynamic 'working-memory occupancy' measure (how many intermediate results are currently live and still needed) and shows that its decay predicts reasoning completion, yielding a novel compression controller grounded in a memory-register view of reasoning.
Abstract: Reasoning models generate long chain-of-thought (CoT) traces, but the amount of information they must actively hold in mind at any instant may be far smaller than the token stream suggests. We hypothesize that a reasoning model maintains a bounded set of 'live' intermediate results in its residual stream, akin to a working-memory register file: a quantity is written when derived, kept live while still needed, and effectively freed once consumed. We propose to measure this live set online. First, we parse CoT into intermediate quantities (numeric values, sub-conclusions) and, for each generation position, train lightweight linear probes to detect whether each previously derived quantity is (a) still linearly decodable ('resident') and (b) still causally needed for the final answer ('live', verified by activation patching). This yields a per-position 'working-memory occupancy' curve. We characterize how occupancy rises and falls across GSM8K, MATH, and ProntoQA on open-weight models (1.5B-8B), testing whether it is bounded and small relative to CoT length, and whether its decay predicts that the answer is imminent. We then build a training-free controller that monitors a cheap online estimate of occupancy and triggers compression—early answer emission when occupancy has been low and stable, or elision of tokens that neither write nor consume live quantities. We evaluate accuracy-vs-tokens Pareto curves against full CoT, fixed truncation, entropy early-exit, and sufficiency-probe baselines, expecting 20-40% token savings at near-equal accuracy plus a mechanistic register-file account of CoT.
Experiments: 1. Quantity extraction: On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B/7B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Llama-3.1-8B, generate full CoT on GSM8K, MATH, ProntoQA. Extract intermediate quantities per step: numeric values/expressions via regex/AST for math, entity-relation sub-conclusions for logic. 2. Residency probes: For each quantity q and each subsequent position t, train a lightweight linear probe on residual-stream hidden states to detect whether q's value is still linearly decodable at t (residency). Report residency lifetimes. 3. Liveness via causal patching: For a sampled set, determine whether q is still causally NEEDED at position t by mean-ablating q's residual signal from t onward and checking answer flips; a quantity that can be ablated without changing the answer is 'freed.' Cross the two signals to define the live set = resident AND causally needed. 4. Occupancy characterization: Compute the per-position count of live quantities ('working-memory occupancy'); test whether it is bounded (small max) and small relative to CoT length; correlate its trajectory (rise, plateau, decay) with difficulty and with distance-to-answer. Test whether sustained low/stable occupancy predicts the answer is near. 5. Online occupancy estimator: Train a small probe/regressor on hidden states to predict current occupancy without per-quantity extraction, enabling a cheap online signal. 6. Compression controller (training-free): (a) early-exit when estimated occupancy stays below a threshold for W consecutive positions (working memory has settled); (b) elide-generation of spans that neither introduce nor consume a live quantity. Sweep thresholds/windows. 7. Evaluation: accuracy vs mean tokens generated (Pareto) and wall-clock latency; baselines: full CoT, fixed truncation, entropy/confidence early-exit, BLADE-style sufficiency exit. Metrics: accuracy, tokens, occupancy-estimator error, fraction compressed, answer-flip rate vs full CoT. 8. Ablations: probe layer, residency-only vs live (residency+liveness), threshold/window sweeps, per-difficulty breakdown, cross-model/cross-dataset transfer of probes and estimator.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Extracting intermediate quantities and defining liveness is noisy, especially for free-form reasoning; we restrict initial analysis to extractable numeric/entity values and validate liveness with causal ablation. 2. Occupancy may not shrink cleanly for problems requiring many simultaneously-held values (hard combinatorics), limiting savings; characterization quantifies this and defines scope. 3. Linear decodability of a quantity is an approximation of residency; causal patching provides the ground truth for liveness. 4. The online occupancy estimator may be inaccurate, causing premature exit; the stability window and Pareto/per-difficulty analyses quantify the risk. 5. Probes and estimator may not transfer across models/datasets, requiring cheap one-time calibration; transfer is tested explicitly. 6. Occupancy could correlate with simpler signals (CoT length, entropy); head-to-head comparison at matched compression tests whether it adds value.
